issues.legal_issue: A transferee already in possession under a mortgage cannot rely on continued possession and acts not unequivocally referable to a concluded written sale contract to obtain protection under the doctrine of part performance.
material_facts: The mortgagee was already in possession under a subsisting mortgage with possession before the alleged sale contract.
The parties disputed whether the proposed sale was conditional or absolute, and the mortgagee relied on an unregistered sale deed as the written contract.
Most of the payment for stamps and registration expenses preceded the alleged written contract, and the remaining payment was not established as an act in furtherance of it.

The mortgagee did not establish other independent acts unequivocally referable to the sale contract and did not perform, or show willingness to perform, his obligations, including paying creditors or the remaining consideration.
issues.conclusion: The mortgagee was not entitled to protection under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, and the mortgagors’ redemption suit was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Section 53A requires a written contract signed by the transferor, with ascertainable transfer terms, possession taken or continued in part performance, an act in furtherance of the contract, and performance or willingness to perform by the transferee. Acts relied on must have a real nexus with, and be unequivocally referable to, the pre-existing contract; preliminary acts and mere retention of possession that is independently justified do not suffice. A payment may support the claim when considered with other acts, but is not automatically part performance. The Court applied Nathulal v. Phool Chand, considered Steadman v. Steadman and Maddison v. Alderson, and relied on the distinction between first entering possession and retaining prior possession reflected in cases including Jahangir Begum v. Gulam Ali Ahmed and Kukali v. Basantilal.

rule.if: redemption_proceeding and transferee_claims_part_performance and claimant_previously_possessed_property and continued_possession_independently_justified and no_independent_act_unequivocally_linked_to_contract and relied_on_acts_preceded_or_were_ambiguous and transferee_failed_to_perform_or_show_willingness

predicates.redemption_proceeding: The dispute is a proceeding seeking redemption of a mortgage over the property.
predicates.transferee_claims_part_performance: A transferee relies on part performance to resist the transferor’s claim concerning the property.
predicates.claimant_previously_possessed_property: The person claiming part-performance protection was in possession before the alleged transfer contract.
predicates.continued_possession_independently_justi: The claimant’s continued possession was supported by an existing legal relationship independent of the alleged transfer contract.
predicates.no_independent_act_unequivocally_linked_: The claimant did not establish an independent act that unequivocally connected the claimant’s conduct to the alleged contract.
predicates.relied_on_acts_preceded_or_were_ambiguou: The acts relied on occurred before the alleged contract or could not be unequivocally attributed to it.
predicates.transferee_failed_to_perform_or_show_wil: The transferee did not perform, or demonstrate willingness to perform, the transferee’s obligations under the contract.

issues.definition: When a transferee already possessed the property on an independent basis, relied on acts that do not unequivocally evidence a concluded contract, and did not perform or show willingness to perform, the transferee cannot use part performance to resist a redemption claim.

issues.legal_issue: A person claiming an interest acquired during a pending property proceeding may be permitted to join or continue the proceeding when the asserted interest has more than a merely colorable basis.
material_facts: A creditor obtained a court sale certificate for the mortgaged property while the mortgagee’s appeal in the redemption litigation was pending.
The creditor applied to be joined, asserting that the court sale had given him an interest in the property and that the litigation would affect that interest.

The chronology of the creditor’s suit, attachment, court sale, and later appellate decree gave the claim more than a mere semblance of title, although the ultimate extent of the interest remained disputed.
issues.conclusion: The creditor’s application was maintainable under Section 146 of the Code of Civil Procedure even if it did not strictly fall within Order XXII Rule 10, and the High Court properly allowed him to be joined.
issues.legal_principle: Order XXII Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits continuation of proceedings by or against a person who acquires an interest by assignment, creation, or devolution during their pendency, with the court’s leave. Section 146 provides an additional basis for an application by a person claiming through or under a party. The Court relied on Smt. Saila Bala Desai v. Smt. Nirmala Sundari Dassi and referred to Shew Bux Mohata v. Bengal Breweries Ltd.

predicates.pending_property_proceeding: A proceeding concerning rights in property is pending when the applicant seeks to participate in it.
predicates.applicant_claims_interest_acquired_durin: The applicant asserts that an interest in the disputed property was acquired while the proceeding was pending.
predicates.claim_has_more_than_colorable_basis: The circumstances asserted by the applicant provide more than a merely nominal basis for claiming an interest, even though the claim’s ultimate merits remain unresolved.

issues.definition: A person asserting an interest acquired during a pending property proceeding may be joined when the circumstances give that asserted interest more than a merely colorable basis.

issues.legal_issue: A decree-holder who purchases attached property at a court auction is not protected as a stranger auction purchaser when the underlying decree is set aside on appeal, and cannot acquire an interest the judgment debtor had already transferred before the auction.
material_facts: The mortgagor transferred the equity of redemption to a subsequent purchaser before the creditor’s court auction.
The creditor had obtained an attachment before judgment and later purchased the property himself at auction while his decree was subject to appeal.
The trial decree was set aside on appeal before a later appellate court restored only a reduced money decree.
The property was sold subject to the subsisting mortgage, and the creditor, rather than an independent stranger, was the auction purchaser.
issues.conclusion: The creditor did not acquire the equity of redemption at the auction and was not entitled to protection as a stranger auction purchaser; his rights did not include ownership of the property.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 64 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a private transfer of attached property is void against claims enforceable under the attachment, which are the claims for which the decree is made. An attachment before judgment serves as security for satisfaction of that claim and falls when the decree supporting it is set aside on appeal. Although a stranger auction purchaser may be protected where execution proceeds without a stay, a decree-holder who purchases with knowledge that the decree is under appeal is not entitled to that protection. The Court followed Janak Raj v. Gurdial Singh and applied Order XXXVIII Rule 5 and Section 64 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

rule.if: appeal_concerning_court_auction_sale and decree_holder_purchased_attached_property and underlying_decree_set_aside_on_appeal and prior_transfer_of_judgment_debtor_interest and property_sold_subject_to_existing_mortgage

predicates.appeal_concerning_court_auction_sale: The proceeding concerns the effect of a court auction conducted to execute a decree that is challenged in appeal.
predicates.decree_holder_purchased_attached_propert: The person who obtained the decree, rather than an independent stranger, purchased the attached property at the court auction.
predicates.underlying_decree_set_aside_on_appeal: The decree being executed was set aside by an appellate court.
predicates.prior_transfer_of_judgment_debtor_intere: The judgment debtor transferred the relevant property interest before the court auction.
predicates.property_sold_subject_to_existing_mortga: The court auction sale was expressly subject to a mortgage that remained in force.

issues.definition: When a decree-holder buys property at auction while the underlying decree is subject to appeal, the decree is set aside, and the judgment debtor had already transferred the interest being sold, the decree-holder does not obtain that interest or the protection available to a stranger purchaser.

issues.legal_issue: A creditor who does not acquire title through a court auction may nevertheless receive an enhanced secured payment where the parties’ conduct has forced the creditor to endure prolonged litigation over an unpaid debt.
material_facts: The creditor’s claim ultimately resulted in a reduced money decree, and his purchase of the property did not give him the equity of redemption.
The mortgagor, subsequent purchaser, and mortgagee had not paid the small debt and allowed the property to be auctioned, requiring the creditor to pursue prolonged litigation.
The creditor’s attachment secured the debt but did not entitle him to retain the property as owner.
issues.conclusion: Taking the parties’ conduct into account, the Court directed that the creditor receive an enhanced amount inclusive of the debt, interest, costs, and litigation costs, secured as a charge on the property payable on redemption.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated attachment as security for the creditor’s enforceable claim, not as a basis for retaining the property, and exercised its equitable authority in light of the parties’ conduct and the prolonged litigation they caused. No separate statutory provision or earlier case was cited as the basis for the enhanced payment.

rule.if: appeal_by_decree_holder_auction_purchaser and claimant_denied_property_title and parties_left_debt_unpaid_and_property_was_auctioned and claimant_endured_prolonged_litigation

predicates.appeal_by_decree_holder_auction_purchase: The proceeding includes an appeal by a creditor who purchased property at an auction held to enforce the creditor’s decree.
predicates.claimant_denied_property_title: The creditor is not permitted to retain the property as its owner.
predicates.parties_left_debt_unpaid_and_property_wa: The parties responsible for the debt left it unpaid, and the property was consequently sold at auction.
predicates.claimant_endured_prolonged_litigation: The creditor was required to pursue prolonged litigation to enforce the debt.

issues.definition: When a creditor is denied title after an auction but the parties’ failure to pay the debt caused an auction and prolonged litigation, the creditor may receive enhanced reimbursement secured against the property.
